## Comparative Evidence Analysis

Experimental comparison must first be organized by protocol rather than by model name. The standard metric-learning episode contains a labeled support set and unlabeled query set from novel classes; reports usually specify the number of ways and shots, such as 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot, because changing either quantity changes task difficulty. A valid within-paper comparison requires the same encoder, training classes, episode sampler, support and query counts, preprocessing, pretraining, and metric. The sources available for this chapter often name datasets and scenarios but do not expose every numeric result or matched implementation detail, so the evidence below compares what each paper measured and does not construct an overall leaderboard. [E:arxiv:1904.04232:section:abstract:8:e517c42438f5:claim:787f0586e85c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a0b05eba6a91] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:20be7fbe9f0c] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:586c6e27983c]

The first comparison dimension is in-domain natural-image evaluation. The metric-learning review identifies the common progression from Siamese and Matching Networks, which compare a query with individual support samples, to prototype methods that summarize support embeddings, and then to distributional or subspace class representations. This is a mechanistic comparison under the same broad episodic setting, but the review excerpt does not provide a common table of accuracies for all three families. Deep Subspace Network is specifically described in that review as more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Network when a class is represented by an SVD-derived low-dimensional subspace and a query is assigned by nearest projected subspace; that robustness claim should not be read as a universal accuracy ranking without the omitted experimental conditions. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:ac1f28b51514] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:09206c2a5f5d] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:6fb92786819f]

Subspace Representation Learning supplies a broader natural-image test across MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and CUB using local CNN feature subspaces, weighted subspace distance, and prototypical or discriminative template subspaces for K-shot aggregation. The paper reports competitive or superior performance relative to prior state-of-the-art methods on those three benchmarks. The useful comparison is that SRL changes both representation and distance geometry rather than only replacing Euclidean distance with another scalar metric; however, the excerpt does not list the exact accuracies, confidence intervals, backbone sizes, or all baselines, so its qualitative result cannot be numerically ranked against prototype, relation-network, or embedding-loss methods evaluated elsewhere. [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:38498384e907] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:e7efc17c96e9]

Embedding-centered methods are best compared on whether representation learning transfers to novel classes. The deep K-tuplet network is trained on miniImageNet and then evaluated on miniImageNet test classes and on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars. Its authors report that it outperforms other metric-based methods and is competitive with other meta-based methods on miniImageNet, while showing substantially better cross-dataset generalization in the introduced cross-domain setting. The comparison supported by the source is therefore between K-tuplet embedding learning and the paper’s selected prior methods under its own training and evaluation protocol; it is not a matched comparison against later ViT, multi-stage, or large-transfer models. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:3aa4a5453197] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:4ec058c0479f] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:7f47a651097d] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:82115d63ae02] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:187c58d813b7]

Proto-Triplet and ICNN losses address the same embedding-separability question with explicit intra-class and inter-class objectives. On miniImageNet, the authors report an accuracy improvement of about two percentage points over compared metric-based few-shot methods, and they also evaluate transfer to CUB, Dogs, and Cars. This result supports the targeted conclusion that shaping embedding geometry can improve a metric-based few-shot classifier in that experimental setup. The two-percentage-point figure is a margin in accuracy as reported by the paper, not a meta-analytic average, and it should not be transferred to K-tuplet, RCN, SRL, or transformer methods unless those models are rerun with the same backbone and episodes. [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:a071b7d26fff] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:d135e3399df7]

Region Comparison Network evaluates a local region-to-region comparison mechanism and its Region Activation Mapping explanations on four benchmark datasets. The paper states that extensive experiments show effectiveness over existing baselines, while its central contribution is to expose which query and support regions contribute to a prediction. Thus RCN should be compared along two axes—classification accuracy and interpretability—not only by top-1 accuracy. The excerpt does not provide the numerical accuracies or identify every baseline, so it supports the existence of a four-benchmark empirical evaluation and an interpretability advantage, but not a numerical claim that region matching beats all later metric learners. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a0b05eba6a91] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:ba8d462b5331] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:0:492c44b3132e:claim:027f4bb4759b]

Global-local and multi-stage embedding methods expand the comparison from one pooled vector to several feature sources. The Siamese Transformer Network uses two self-supervised ViT-Small branches, Euclidean distance for global features, KL divergence for local features, normalization, and weighted fusion; it reports superior performance to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot benchmarks in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings. MSENet uses multi-stage outputs, self-attention, and learnable stage weights, and evaluates 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot tasks on MiniImageNet and FC100 plus cross-domain tasks across eight datasets. Both support the value of richer features, but their results are not directly comparable to CNN methods unless ViT pretraining, self-supervised initialization, branch parameters, training data, and the exact benchmark baselines are matched. [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:0d288a085200] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:87dac66782d0]

Cross-domain evaluation introduces a separate axis that can reverse conclusions drawn from in-domain splits. The feature-wise transformation study argues that metric functions can overfit feature distributions from seen domains and fail on unseen domains; it tests domain-generalized novel-category recognition and presents layers that can be inserted into different metric-based approaches. This makes the relevant baseline a metric model with and without feature distribution modulation, rather than a comparison between Euclidean distance and a learned relation module in isolation. The paper also notes that transformation hyperparameters can require careful hand-tuning, so any gain must be interpreted together with the added tuning and domain-randomization mechanism. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:ba5104371383] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:586c6e27983c]

Task structure is another experimental dimension. Meta-Metric-Learner is evaluated not only in the standard k-shot N-way setting but also in a realistic setting with flexible numbers of classes, in both single-source and multi-source forms. Its authors report superior performance across these settings. This evidence directly addresses flexibility: a fixed task-invariant metric is convenient when tasks are similar, while a meta-specified task-specific metric is designed to handle varying class counts and broader task distributions. These flexible-task numbers cannot be compared with ordinary fixed 5-way miniImageNet scores because the episode structure and source-domain conditions differ. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:dd816f2ea86d] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:9f83023d956c]

Cross-family and modality-specific results further constrain ranking. The VTAB+Meta-Dataset study finds that large-scale BiT transfer is, on average, stronger than competing approaches on Meta-Dataset and is a robust few-shot baseline, while meta-learners struggle on VTAB when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset; it also reports that increasing scale does not help highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks. This is a transfer-versus-meta evaluation under deliberately broad protocols, not proof that metric learning is inferior. In the FewSAR benchmark, metric-learning methods achieve the best accuracy under the unified SAR setting, while meta-learning and fine-tuning perform poorly; in hyperspectral cross-domain work, multi-level relation learning improves over the cited state of the art. Because SAR, hyperspectral, Meta-Dataset, VTAB, miniImageNet, and CUB differ in sensors, domains, scale, and adaptation rules, these findings are evidence of protocol dependence and must not be merged into one cross-dataset ranking. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The first open problem is that metric learning does not remove the fundamental few-shot data limitation; it relocates it into the learned embedding, class representation, and comparison function. With only one to five labeled support examples, a conventional classifier can overfit, but point prototypes and individual exemplars can also be unstable when those examples are noisy, atypical, or insufficient to span class variation. Distributional and subspace methods explicitly target this weakness by modeling uncertainty, variation, or geometric structure, yet they must estimate those structures from the same scarce support set, so robustness is an assumption supported only under suitable data and estimation conditions. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:d81b27db6161] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:ac1f28b51514] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:09206c2a5f5d] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:38498384e907]

A second problem is choosing the right class representation without knowing the geometry of a novel class. Exemplar comparisons preserve individual support images but offer little aggregation; prototypes provide a compact mean-like summary but can collapse multimodal classes; distributions express uncertainty but require reliable distribution estimates; subspaces preserve variation or spatial structure but introduce singular-value decomposition, dimensionality, and template construction choices. These alternatives are complementary modeling biases, not a guaranteed progression toward a universally better classifier. The available evidence supports robustness or competitive accuracy for particular subspace and distributional designs, but not the conclusion that every few-shot class should be represented as a distribution or subspace. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:ac1f28b51514] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:09206c2a5f5d] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:38498384e907] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:e7efc17c96e9]

The comparison function creates a related flexibility–generalization trade-off. Fixed Euclidean, cosine, nearest-prototype, or nearest-subspace rules are simple and stable, but they presuppose that one task-invariant geometric relation remains valid across episodes and classes. Learned nonlinear relation modules can express more complex compatibility between query and support features, but their extra capacity is trained on episodic tasks and must transfer to unseen classes; a scalar learned relation score is also less directly geometric than an explicit distance. Metric-agnostic conditional networks show that query-conditioned neural classifiers can perform well, but their authors distinguish that softmax-score architecture from a true metric, so it should be treated as a relational alternative rather than evidence that geometric comparison is obsolete. [E:arxiv:1904.04232:section:abstract:8:e517c42438f5:claim:787f0586e85c] [E:arxiv:1711.06025:section:abstract:4:b851ec357ca4:claim:d8c9d9457f22] [E:arxiv:1711.06025:section:abstract:19:ad703728289e:claim:fddf369f93f3] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:2:c37dc575d3c8:claim:c2148ed1f828] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:9f83023d956c]

Domain shift remains a concrete failure mode even when a metric succeeds on novel classes from the same benchmark. Metric-based encoders and metric functions can overfit feature distributions seen during episodic training and then fail on unseen domains; this is distinct from ordinary novel-class split generalization because image-feature distributions themselves change. Feature-wise transformation layers address the problem by simulating varied feature distributions and are described as method-agnostic add-ons for metric-based approaches, but the source also reports that their hyperparameters may require meticulous hand-tuning because cross-domain feature variation is difficult to model. Thus domain modulation adds both a potential robustness benefit and a tuning burden. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:586c6e27983c] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:2:ada74c4d4774:claim:ba5104371383]

Evaluation fragmentation limits scientific comparison across the metric-learning literature. Papers report miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, CUB, Caltech-101, Dogs, Cars, FC100, Meta-Dataset, VTAB, SAR, and hyperspectral tasks, with different 1-shot or 5-shot, N-way, backbone, pretraining, episode-sampling, and adaptation settings. A gain on one protocol—such as the reported roughly two-percentage-point miniImageNet improvement from Proto-Triplet or ICNN losses, K-tuplet cross-dataset results, or best accuracy for metric methods in the FewSAR setting—cannot be converted into a general ranking when the methods were not run under matched data, architecture, and training budgets. This is a limitation of comparability, not proof that a missing method is ineffective. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:3aa4a5453197] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:4ec058c0479f] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:a071b7d26fff] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:d135e3399df7] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:38498384e907] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:cec40219d8a6] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:a072e9d31497]

Cross-family evaluation adds another unresolved issue: episodic metric learners and large-scale transfer learners optimize under different assumptions. The VTAB+Meta-Dataset study reports that carefully engineered large-scale BiT pretraining and fine-tuning is a remarkably competitive and robust few-shot baseline, and that BiT on average outperforms competing approaches on Meta-Dataset, while meta-learning approaches struggle on VTAB when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset. The same study also finds that pushing scale does not improve highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks. Consequently, neither small episodic benchmark results nor large transfer results alone establish which metric mechanism is best; matched data scale, model capacity, fine-tuning, and test distribution are necessary for a fair comparison. [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:a072e9d31497] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:45:924c867b4c98:claim:cf4588225598] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:45:924c867b4c98:claim:64f80245fb9d] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:9:1354132472a1:claim:ddef54f47d25] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:c92e388de5e0:claim:258ac9920e99]

Richer embeddings improve available cues but impose their own costs and dependencies. K-tuplet and margin-style losses require informative sampling or careful intra-class and inter-class objectives; multi-stage networks add multiple outputs, self-attention, and learnable stage weights; global-local ViT branches add parameters and depend on pretrained, self-supervised features. These designs can counter the loss of shallow, local, or abstract information when a single pooled vector and single distance are used, but the source evidence does not imply that added branches always improve accuracy. Their trade-offs include training complexity, pretraining dependence, fusion-weight selection, and the risk of fitting benchmark-specific feature combinations. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:82115d63ae02] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:187c58d813b7] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:a071b7d26fff] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:87dac66782d0] [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:0d288a085200]

Interpretability is still incomplete even for spatially explicit metric learners. Region Comparison Network and Region Activation Mapping make query-support region correspondence more visible and extend explanation toward category-level prototypical parts, addressing the difficulty of understanding which support and query image regions influence a decision. Visual correspondence is nevertheless an explanation of internal comparison, not by itself a causal guarantee that the highlighted regions are the sole or correct basis for classification. Metric methods therefore need both region-level evidence and controlled evaluation if interpretability claims are to support deployment decisions. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a0b05eba6a91] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:ba8d462b5331] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:0:492c44b3132e:claim:027f4bb4759b]

Task heterogeneity challenges the common assumption of one shared metric across all episodes. A fixed metric can accommodate different class counts more naturally than some parameter-prediction meta-learners, but the Meta-Metric-Learner paper argues that a task-invariant metric is most plausible when tasks come from similar domains; realistic episodes may vary in class number, source domain, and task distribution. Its hybrid solution uses a meta-learner to specify a task-specific metric-based learner, improving flexibility at the cost of additional meta-learning machinery. This leaves an open choice between simple transferable metrics and adaptive metrics: the former are easier to deploy and inspect, while the latter require evidence that adaptation generalizes rather than overfits the training task distribution. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:9f83023d956c] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:dd816f2ea86d] [E:arxiv:1904.04232:section:abstract:8:e517c42438f5:claim:787f0586e85c]

Finally, modality-specific success should not be mistaken for a universal solution. Multi-level contrastive and cross-attention relation learning is motivated and evaluated for cross-domain few-shot hyperspectral images, while FewSAR reports favorable metric-learning accuracy under its unified SAR protocol; both sensor settings have data characteristics and dataset biases different from natural-image benchmarks. Likewise, zero-shot metric learning uses class descriptions or attributes rather than a labeled support image and therefore answers a related but distinct recognition problem. Future comparisons should preserve these task boundaries, report matched in-domain and cross-domain results, and state representation, metric, backbone, pretraining, adaptation, tuning, and uncertainty conditions before claiming broad superiority. ## Conclusion

No single metric-learning mechanism is universally best: prototypes suit compact point-like classes, distributions and subspaces address uncertainty or structured variation, region and global-local embeddings exploit local or multi-level cues, and fixed versus learned comparators trade simplicity for flexibility. These choices should be matched to class geometry, domain shift, task heterogeneity, interpretability needs and available pretraining, rather than inferred from model family alone. The main practical answer is therefore conditional. Metric learning remains useful because it transfers similarity-based prediction to novel classes without fitting a large conventional classifier to one to five labels, but it does not eliminate data scarcity. Fair comparison requires matched episodic protocols, architectures, training data and adaptation rules; under the cited unmatched settings, the evidence supports qualified advantages and trade-offs, not a general ranking over metric, meta-learning or large-scale transfer approaches. issues.explanation: The claim that BiT-style approaches 'pretrain a large network on upstream data and fine-tune downstream' is not supported by the cited sources: c4 and c22 (arxiv:2104.02638) describe BiT as a competitive large-scale transfer baseline but do not state the pretrain-then-fine-tune pipeline, and c28 (arxiv:2104.02638) discusses transfer learners generally without specifying BiT's training procedure. The pipeline description is an unsupported inference about BiT's method.

The statement that 'meta-learners struggle on VTAB when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset' is attributed to c36, but c36 (arxiv:2104.02638) states that 'meta-learning approaches struggle to compete on VTAB when trained and validated on MD' — the cited source does not use the word 'struggle' in the way the draft presents it, and the draft omits the source's qualifier that this is a cross-family evaluation under deliberately broad protocols. The claim is presented as a direct finding without the source's framing.

The claim that 'BiT on average outperforms competing approaches on Meta-Dataset' is attributed to c36, but c36 (arxiv:2104.02638) states that 'on average, large-scale transfer methods (Big Transfer, BiT) outperform competing approaches on MD, even when trained only on ImageNet.' The draft correctly captures this, but the unit also states that 'meta-learning approaches struggle on VTAB when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset' — this is a separate claim from c36 that is presented without the source's explicit framing as a cross-family evaluation result, and the draft does not distinguish it from the BiT finding.

The claim that the multi-level relation method 'builds on a domain-discriminator approach, adds contrastive learning for class-level sample relations, and uses transformer cross-attention to model set-level relations from queries to supports' is attributed to c20 (arxiv:2311.01212). The source states that the method 'applies contrastive learning to learn the class-level sample relations' and 'adopts a transformer based cross-attention learning module to learn the set-level sample relations and acquire the attention from query samples to support samples,' but the draft's phrasing 'builds on a domain-discriminator approach' is an inference not explicitly stated in the cited excerpt — the source says it 'builds on current method of Deep Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning for Hyperspectral Image Classification which adopts a domain discriminator,' but the draft presents this as a direct claim without the source's framing.

The abstract states that 'reported gains include stronger cross-dataset generalization for deep K-tuplet learning' — this is attributed to c12, c29, c8, c17, c23, c26, c27, but c12 and c29 (SRL) do not report cross-dataset generalization; they report competitive/superior performance on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and CUB. The cross-dataset claim is supported by c8, c17, c23, c26, c27 (K-tuplet), but the abstract bundles c12 and c29 into the same sentence, implying SRL also reports cross-dataset gains, which is not supported by the cited sources.

The claim that MSENet 'evaluates 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot tasks on MiniImageNet and FC100 plus cross-domain tasks across eight datasets' is attributed to c9 (arxiv:2409.07989). The source states that MSENet was evaluated on 'MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets, specifically in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios' and 'cross-domain tasks across eight benchmark datasets,' but the draft presents this as a direct finding without noting that the source does not provide numerical accuracies or identify all baselines — the unit correctly notes this limitation, but the claim that MSENet 'achieves high accuracy in the testing domains' is presented as a direct result, while the source only states that evaluations 'demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in comparison to state-of-the-art approaches' without providing specific numbers.

review.explanation: The draft is generally well-structured and source-grounded, with most claims properly attributed. The identified issues involve unsupported inferences about BiT's training pipeline, misattribution of cross-dataset claims to SRL, and presentation of source findings without their original framing qualifiers. These are bounded attribution and framing problems rather than wholesale fabrication.

claim_records.text: The proposed Metric-Agnostic Conditional network (MACO) architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD birds fine-grained classification task.

The MACO architecture replaces the metric space comparison used in traditional metric-learning few-shot approaches with a learned neural network, outputting a softmax probability distribution rather than a true distance or similarity metric.

The MACO network achieves its best performance only when it is allowed to condition each class representation based on the target query image; the metric-agnostic aspect alone is not sufficient for good performance.

The MACO feature stage uses four convolutional blocks, each with a 3×3 kernel, 32 filters, batch normalization, ELU activation, and 2×2 max pooling, followed by a linear layer producing an 800-dimensional image feature vector.

The MACO relational stage uses pairwise comparisons of images within each support set class via a relational network, producing a single order-insensitive vector representation for each class with parameters shared across all classes.
Traditional metric-learning few-shot approaches rely on pre-defined distance metrics such as Euclidean or cosine distance to separate classes within a learned metric space.

claim_records.text: The proposed Meta-Metric-Learner hybrid model combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning approaches, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner model is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

Experiments show the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot setting and the new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in single-source and multi-source forms.

Existing optimization-based few-shot learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, and thus can only handle tasks that share a uniform number of classes.
Existing metric-based few-shot learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, and require tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.

The Meta-Metric-Learner meta learner uses an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners, while the base learner exploits a metric-based model parameterized by weight predictions from the optimization-based meta-learner.

The Meta-Metric-Learner model can handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets and generate task-specific metrics that adapt better to different tasks by leveraging weight prediction from the meta-learner given task instances.

claim_records.text: Simon et al. proposed Deep Subspace Network (DSN) to represent each class using a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples via singular value decomposition.

DSN classifies query samples according to the nearest subspace classifier, assigning the query to the class which has the shortest Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto the class-specific subspace.
DSN is shown to be more robust to noises and outliers than Prototypical Network.
Few-shot classification aims to learn a classification rule from few (typically 1-5) labeled examples.
The biggest challenge in few-shot classification is a high risk of model overfitting to the few labeled training samples.
Meta-learning methods train a meta-learner on many different classification tasks to extract generalizable knowledge, enabling rapid learning on a new related task with few examples.
Transfer learning methods presume shared knowledge between the source and target domains, and fine-tune the model trained on abundant source data to fit few labeled target samples.

Metric learning methods learn feature embeddings and/or distance measures, and classify an unseen sample based on its distance to labeled samples or class representations, with samples of the same class expected to locate close together in the embedding space and samples of different classes far apart.
Meta-learning, transfer learning, and metric learning methods can be applied simultaneously, for example learning feature embeddings of metric learning methods by using a meta-learning strategy.

fact_fields.method: review of deep metric learning methods

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset, and query images of the novel class are classified by computing their distances to novel support images with respect to the learned measure, followed by applying a distance-based classifier.

fact_fields.method: supervised metric learning for few-shot classification

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: Early few-shot metric learning methods such as Siamese Network and Matching Network classify a query sample by measuring and comparing its distance to support samples.

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: Class prototypes serve as reference vectors for each class, and can be constructed by taking simple or weighted average of feature embeddings, or learned in an end-to-end manner to improve representation ability.

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: Zhang et al. proposed a variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning that uses the Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure the distance of samples and computes the confidence that a query image is assigned into each class by estimating the distribution of each class based on a neural network.

fact_fields.method: variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: Simon et al. proposed Deep Subspace Network (DSN) to represent each class using a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples via singular value decomposition.

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: DSN classifies query samples according to the nearest subspace classifier, assigning the query to the class which has the shortest Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto the class-specific subspace.

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: DSN is shown to be more robust to noises and outliers than Prototypical Network.

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: The biggest challenge in few-shot classification is a high risk of model overfitting to the few labeled training samples.

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: Meta-learning methods train a meta-learner on many different classification tasks to extract generalizable knowledge, enabling rapid learning on a new related task with few examples.

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: Transfer learning methods presume shared knowledge between the source and target domains, and fine-tune the model trained on abundant source data to fit few labeled target samples.

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: Metric learning methods learn feature embeddings and/or distance measures, and classify an unseen sample based on its distance to labeled samples or class representations, with samples of the same class expected to locate close together in the embedding space and samples of different classes far apart.

evidence_items.paper_title: Deep Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: A Review of Recent Developments
evidence_items.claim_text: Meta-learning, transfer learning, and metric learning methods can be applied simultaneously, for example learning feature embeddings of metric learning methods by using a meta-learning strategy.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-prototype similarity and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for image classification.

To alleviate the influence of observation noises on the similarity of a query-prototype pair, the similarity between a query feature zi and a prototype feature cj is modeled by a distribution (probabilistic similarity) based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation, rather than a scalar.

For a query sample xi and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is taken as a node and a graph-based model is employed to jointly infer the similarity uncertainty σi,j for each query-prototype pair.
The network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses which exploit the estimated similarity uncertainty.
Few-shot image classification aims to classify query samples of new categories given only a few labeled support samples of these categories as examples.

In similarity-based few-shot image classification, the set of category-specific prototypes (average feature embeddings of support samples per category) acts as a similarity-based classifier to identify the category of a query sample by finding the nearest prototype over the support set in the embedding space.

During training of similarity-based few-shot image classification, the logit vector (classification probability) for a query sample is obtained by feeding the similarities between the query sample and the prototypes to a SoftMax function.
Aleatoric uncertainty identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample, capturing the noise inherent in the observations.

For few-shot image classification, the network has different uncertainties on the calculated similarities of different query-prototype pairs, and an observed similarity of a query-prototype pair (being a one time sampling) suffers from observation noise, where higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.
For each few-shot task during optimization, the number of experienced query-prototype pairs is limited, so the side effect of observation noises due to high uncertainty limits optimization.

In the proposed uncertainty-aware few-shot image classification framework, for each query-prototype pair, the observed feature similarity between the query and the prototype is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the variance of this distribution characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.
The similarity-based classification losses are calculated based on the probabilistic similarity representations with estimated uncertainty for query-prototype pairs.
The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot framework for image classification models uncertainty of the similarities of query-support pairs and performs uncertainty-aware optimization.
The UAFS method exploits similarity uncertainty by converting observed similarities to probabilistic representations and incorporating them to the loss for more effective optimization.

fact_fields.method: probabilistic similarity representation conversion for loss optimization

claim_records.text: A graph-based model is utilized to estimate the uncertainty of query-support pair similarities in order to jointly consider the similarities between a query and the prototypes in a support set.
Extensive experiments show the proposed UAFS method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

claim_records.text: Existing metric-based few-shot classification algorithms often fail to generalize to unseen domains due to large discrepancy of the feature distribution across domains.

The core idea of the proposed method is to use feature-wise transformation layers for augmenting image features using affine transforms to simulate various feature distributions under different domains in the training stage.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layers with affine transforms

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn approach is applied to search for the hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers to capture variations of the feature distributions under different domains.
Extensive experiments and ablation studies are conducted under the domain generalization setting using five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models, and provides consistent improvements on the few-shot classification performance under domain shift.
Metric-based meta-learning models usually consist of a feature encoder E and metric function M.
The key observation of the work is that the distributions of the image features extracted from tasks in the unseen domains are significantly different from those in the seen domains.
During the training stage, the metric function may overfit to the feature distributions encoded only from the seen domains and thus fail to generalize to unseen domains.

The proposed method integrates feature-wise transformation layers to modulate feature activations with affine transformations into the feature encoder, to simulate various distributions of image features during the training stage and improve the generalization ability of the metric function in the testing phase.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layer integration into feature encoder

claim_records.text: The hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers may require meticulous hand-tuning due to the difficulty to model the complex variation of the image feature distributions across various domains.

A learning-to-learn algorithm is developed to optimize the proposed feature-wise transformation layers, with the core idea of optimizing the layers so that the model can work well on unseen domains after training using seen domains.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layers are method-agnostic and can be applied to various metric-based few-shot classification approaches for improving their generalization to unseen domains.
Metric-based few-shot classification methods make predictions based on the similarity between the query image and support examples.

Given an input task consisting of few labeled support images and unlabeled query images from novel classes, the encoder first extracts image features, and the metric function then takes features of both labeled and unlabeled images as input and predicts the category of the query images.
Existing metric-based approaches do not generalize well to categories from different domains, as raised by Chen et al. (2019a).

claim_records.text: Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method proposed for few-shot image classification that aims to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify specific mutually related regions in query and support set images.

fact_fields.method: Region Comparison Network (RCN), a metric learning based method

claim_records.text: Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy designed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
The proposed method generalizes interpretability from the task level to the category level, which can be viewed as a way to find prototypical parts that support RCN's final decision.
Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RCN method over existing baselines.

Few-shot learning aims to learn a classifier for a set of classes using only limited labeled training samples, and has attracted increasing research attention due to the high cost of large-scale labeled data annotation.

Existing few-shot learning works are grouped into metric-based models and gradient-based models, with metric-based methods addressing the problem by computing similarity between support and query samples using metric methods such as Euclidean distance.
The RCN model generates a region weight in its final stage to define which common parts between support and query samples most influence the final similarity score.

Compared to attention mechanisms, RCN directly indicates the relationship between final classification decisions and region similarities in the last layer as a simple, easily explained linear process.
The region meta learner in RCN is a dynamic system designed to adapt to different meta tasks during both the training and testing stages.
RAM visualizes the weight and similarity scores of regions to intuitively show the interpretability of the RCN model.
A statistic-based method is presented to generalize and quantify RCN's explanations into a set of standard rules for the comparison process, alongside a generalization method to find prototypes.

claim_records.text: VTAB+MD is a proposed few-shot classification evaluation protocol designed to facilitate idea exchange and comparison between the transfer learning and few-shot classification communities.

A carefully engineered training and fine-tuning pipeline for large-scale networks, exemplified by BiT, is a remarkably competitive and robust baseline for few-shot classification that generalizes across large-scale, multi-dataset benchmarks.

fact_fields.method: Big Transfer (BiT) large-scale network training and fine-tuning

claim_records.text: On average, large-scale transfer methods (Big Transfer, BiT) outperform competing approaches on the Meta-Dataset (MD) benchmark, even when trained only on ImageNet.
Meta-learning approaches struggle to compete on the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark (VTAB) when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset (MD).
Increasing model scale does not improve BiT performance on highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks.

Transfer learning approaches for few-shot classification involve first pre-training a model on an upstream dataset (e.g. ImageNet) and later fine-tuning it on different downstream tasks, and are best exemplified when limited downstream data is available.

fact_fields.method: Transfer learning pipeline for few-shot classification

claim_records.text: Several recent papers report that well-tuned transfer learning baselines are competitive with more complex few-shot classification approaches.

Applying the established Meta-Dataset few-shot classification evaluation protocol to large-scale (data and capacity) transfer learners highlights limitations of episodic approaches and reveals where transfer learning falls short.

evidence_items.claim_text: VTAB+MD is a proposed few-shot classification evaluation protocol designed to facilitate idea exchange and comparison between the transfer learning and few-shot classification communities.

evidence_items.paper_title: Comparing Transfer and Meta Learning Approaches on a Unified Few-Shot Classification Benchmark
evidence_items.claim_text: A carefully engineered training and fine-tuning pipeline for large-scale networks, exemplified by BiT, is a remarkably competitive and robust baseline for few-shot classification that generalizes across large-scale, multi-dataset benchmarks.

fact_fields.method: Big Transfer (BiT) large-scale network training and fine-tuning

evidence_items.paper_title: Comparing Transfer and Meta Learning Approaches on a Unified Few-Shot Classification Benchmark
evidence_items.claim_text: On average, large-scale transfer methods (Big Transfer, BiT) outperform competing approaches on the Meta-Dataset (MD) benchmark, even when trained only on ImageNet.

evidence_items.paper_title: Comparing Transfer and Meta Learning Approaches on a Unified Few-Shot Classification Benchmark
evidence_items.claim_text: Meta-learning approaches struggle to compete on the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark (VTAB) when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset (MD).

evidence_items.paper_title: Comparing Transfer and Meta Learning Approaches on a Unified Few-Shot Classification Benchmark
evidence_items.claim_text: Increasing model scale does not improve BiT performance on highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks.

evidence_items.paper_title: Comparing Transfer and Meta Learning Approaches on a Unified Few-Shot Classification Benchmark
evidence_items.claim_text: Transfer learning approaches for few-shot classification involve first pre-training a model on an upstream dataset (e.g. ImageNet) and later fine-tuning it on different downstream tasks, and are best exemplified when limited downstream data is available.

fact_fields.method: Transfer learning pipeline for few-shot classification

evidence_items.paper_title: Comparing Transfer and Meta Learning Approaches on a Unified Few-Shot Classification Benchmark
evidence_items.claim_text: Several recent papers report that well-tuned transfer learning baselines are competitive with more complex few-shot classification approaches.

evidence_items.paper_title: Comparing Transfer and Meta Learning Approaches on a Unified Few-Shot Classification Benchmark
evidence_items.claim_text: Applying the established Meta-Dataset few-shot classification evaluation protocol to large-scale (data and capacity) transfer learners highlights limitations of episodic approaches and reveals where transfer learning falls short.

fact_fields.method: Cross-family evaluation of transfer learners on Meta-Dataset protocol

claim_records.text: The Relation Network (RN) is trained end-to-end from scratch, and during meta-learning it learns a deep distance metric to compare images within episodes designed to simulate the few-shot setting.
Once trained, a Relation Network can classify images of new classes by computing relation scores between query images and the few examples of each new class without further updating the network.

The Relation Network framework is easily extended to zero-shot learning, and extensive experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate it provides a unified and effective approach for both few-shot and zero-shot learning.

The Relation Network training objective uses mean squared error (MSE) to minimize the difference between predicted relation scores and ground-truth targets, where matched pairs have similarity 1 and mismatched pairs have similarity 0.

The relation module of the Relation Network consists of two convolutional blocks and two fully-connected layers; each convolutional block is a 3×3 convolution with 64 filters followed by batch normalisation, ReLU non-linearity and 2×2 max-pooling.
The output size of the last max pooling layer in the Relation Network relation module is H=64 for Omniglot, and H=64*3*3=576 for miniImageNet.

The two fully-connected layers in the Relation Network relation module are 8-dimensional and 1-dimensional respectively; all fully-connected layers use ReLU except the output layer which uses Sigmoid to generate relation scores.
For zero-shot learning, the Relation Network uses an existing pretrained DNN subnet (e.g., Inception or ResNet) pretrained on ImageNet.

Few-shot recognition experiments evaluate the Relation Network on Omniglot and miniImageNet for few-shot classification, and on Animals with Attributes (AwA) and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB) for zero-shot classification.

Few-shot learning experiments use Adam optimizer with initial learning rate 1e-3, annealed by half for every 100,000 episodes, and all models are end-to-end trained from scratch with no additional dataset.
The Omniglot dataset contains 1623 character classes from 50 different alphabets, each class containing 20 samples drawn by different people.

Following prior work, new Omniglot classes are augmented via 90°, 180° and 270° rotations of existing data; 1200 original classes plus rotations are used for training, and the remaining 423 classes plus rotations are used for testing, with all input images resized to 28×28.

Unlike prior few-shot learning approaches that learn a transferable embedding and pre-define a fixed metric such as Euclidean distance, the Relation Network further aims to learn a transferable deep metric for comparing relations between images (few-shot) or between images and class descriptions (zero-shot).
Zero-shot learning is analogous to one-shot learning, except the support set contains a semantic class embedding vector vc for each class instead of a one-shot image per class.

Baselines compared against in few-shot recognition experiments include neural statistician, Matching Nets with and without fine-tuning, MANN, Siamese Nets with Memory, Convolutional Siamese Nets, MAML, Meta Nets, Prototypical Nets and Meta-Learner LSTM.

claim_records.text: Existing CLIP-based few-shot classification approaches such as CoOp and Tip-Adapter only focus on high-level visual features that are fully aligned with textual features representing the 'Summary' of the image.
Compared with high-level representations, low-level local representations (LRs) are more consistent between seen and unseen samples of the same category.
The proposed Meta-Feature Adaption method (MF-Adapter) combines complementary strengths of both low-level local representations and high-level semantic representations.
The Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric to measure category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
An MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to adequately generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.

Extensive experiments show the proposed MF-Adapter method is superior to state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, with stronger performance on a set of challenging visual classification tasks.
CLIP and ALIGN are pre-trained vision-language models that learn high-quality visual representation by conducting contrastive learning with hundreds of millions of noisy text-image pairs.
In few-shot classification where seen images are insufficient, simply adopting the standard 'pre-training&fine-tuning' paradigm does not produce better results.
Common practice for few-shot CLIP adaptation is to fix CLIP pre-training weights while learning a lightweight module on top of CLIP.
Prompt-based methods such as CoOp and CoCoOp learn continuous text prompts to replace manually set prompts with trainable parameters, achieving improvements over manually tuned prompts.

Adapter-based methods such as CLIP-Adapter and Tip-Adapter only fine-tune a small number of additional linear layers on top of CLIP; Tip-Adapter fine-tunes a trainable query-key cache layer and achieves large performance compared to both prompt-based methods and CLIP-Adapter on several classification datasets.

MF-Unit is obtained by an inductive representation of local feature maps on different scales using sliding windows with different perceptual fields, containing rich local information to represent category-consistent characteristics.
The global feature representation from the final layer of CLIP's ResNet-50 is a 1024-dimensional feature vector.

fact_fields.method: CLIP ResNet-50 final layer feature extraction

claim_records.text: Before model training, support set images are encoded into different-level features by the fixed CLIP visual encoder, then low-level feature maps are unfolded into Meta-Feature using a list of sliding windows with different scales.

MF-Unit is calculated by inductive max and mean operations on each sliding window to compress parameters and reduce redundancy, and is regarded as category-consistent features containing inductive knowledge.

During inference, the MF-Adapter model first infers test images into MF-Units at different levels and different scales, then retrieves few-shot knowledge in the MF-Unit space of the support set to obtain local logits.
The final MF-Adapter prediction combines the local logits from MF-Unit retrieval with the original CLIP's high-level prediction, similar to Tip-Adapter.
The MF-Adapter method is the first work to utilize the local similarity of CLIP in few-shot learning.
Comprehensive experiments on 11 widely-adopted datasets for few-shot classification demonstrate that MF-Adapter achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with previous CLIP-based methods.

CLIP and ALIGN leverage hundreds of millions of image-text pairs collected from the internet to align the embedding space of images with raw texts, and have demonstrated strong performance on zero-shot image classification tasks.
On top of CLIP, recent few-shot learning adaptation methods are roughly divided into two types: prompt-based methods and adapter-based methods.
Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) achieved significant performance gains by introducing a small amount of task-specific prompts for computer vision few-shot adaptation.

claim_records.text: Prototypical networks learn a metric space in which classification can be performed by computing distances to prototype representations of each class for few-shot classification.
Prototypical networks achieve state-of-the-art results on the CU-Birds dataset when extended to zero-shot learning.
Prototypical networks differ from matching networks in the few-shot case, and become equivalent to matching networks in the one-shot scenario.

fact_fields.method: Comparison between prototypical networks and matching networks

claim_records.text: When squared Euclidean distance is used, prototypical networks produce a linear classifier, while matching networks produce a weighted nearest neighbor classifier given the support set.

fact_fields.method: Comparison between prototypical networks and matching networks

claim_records.text: Matching networks use an attention mechanism over a learned embedding of the labeled support set to predict classes for unlabeled query points.
Matching networks utilize sampled mini-batches called episodes during training, where each episode subsamples classes and data points to mimic the few-shot task.
Ravi and Larochelle propose a meta-learning approach to few-shot learning that trains an LSTM to produce updates to a classifier given an episode.
Prototypical networks naturally generalize to other distance functions, particularly Bregman divergences, and only require one prototype per class.

Matching networks and prototypical networks can be seen as forms of meta-learning, as they produce simple classifiers dynamically from new training episodes, while their core embeddings are fixed after training.

fact_fields.method: Comparison between matching networks, prototypical networks and meta-learning

claim_records.text: Prototypical networks are related to clustering, and class means are justified as prototypes when distances are computed with a Bregman divergence such as squared Euclidean distance.
Euclidean distance greatly outperforms the more commonly used cosine similarity for prototypical networks.
Prototypical networks achieve state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark tasks for few-shot and zero-shot learning.
Prototypical networks produce a discriminative summary statistic for each class, unlike the neural statistician which produces an approximate posterior over a statistic vector.

fact_fields.method: Comparison between prototypical networks and neural statistician

claim_records.text: The proposed subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image using a subspace in local CNN feature space, and measures similarity between two images via a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available per class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation, in contrast to most previous works that adopted global vector representation, can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image.
Experiments on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB) demonstrate competitive or superior performance of the SRL framework compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.

claim_records.text: The proposed Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes for few-shot learning.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function of the ADM network.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic in comparison to image classification.

fact_fields.method: comparison of ranking relation classification to image classification

claim_records.text: The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes as input an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products, and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with the query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: DeepEMD employs the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) as a metric to compute a structural distance between dense image representations to determine image relevance.
The EMD generates the optimal matching flows between structural elements that have the minimum matching cost, which is used to calculate the image distance for classification.

DeepEMD designs a cross-reference mechanism to generate the important weights of elements in the EMD formulation, which can effectively alleviate the adverse impact caused by the cluttered background and large intra-class appearance variations.
To implement k-shot classification, DeepEMD proposes to learn a structured fully connected layer that can directly classify dense image representations with the EMD.
Based on the implicit function theorem, the EMD can be inserted as a layer into the network for end-to-end training.

DeepEMD outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin on five widely used few-shot classification benchmarks: miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Fewshot-CIFAR100 (FC100), Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB), and CIFAR-FewShot (CIFAR-FS).
DeepEMD demonstrates effectiveness on the image retrieval task in experiments.
Cluttered background and large intra-class appearance variations may drive the image-level embeddings from the same category far apart in a given metric space.
DeepEMD uses an optimal matching cost between image regions to represent the image distance more faithfully.
DeepEMD formulates one-shot classification as an optimal matching problem that can be trained end-to-end.
DeepEMD's model with EMD as the distance metric significantly outperforms baseline models based on image-level representations and local representations for 1-shot classification.

fact_fields.method: DeepEMD with EMD as distance metric

claim_records.text: DeepEMD's algorithm on both 1-shot and 5-shot classification tasks significantly outperforms baseline methods and achieves new state-of-the-art performance on miniImagenet, tieredImagenet, FC100, CUB, and CIFAR-FS.
DeepEMD can effectively improve many deep metric learning methods on the image retrieval task.

claim_records.text: The proposed unified Query-Support TransFormer (QSFormer) model simultaneously models consistent support/query image representations and effective cross-set metric learning for few-shot classification.
The QSFormer sampleFormer branch adopts Encoder, Decoder and Cross-Attention to respectively model Support representation, Query image representation, and metric learning for few-shot classification.

QSFormer includes a local patch Transformer branch that extracts structural representation for each image sample by capturing long-range dependence of local image patches, as a complement to the global sampleFormer branch.
A novel Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor (CIFE) is proposed to extract and fuse multi-scale CNN features as the backbone module for the QSFormer few-shot learning method.
All modules of QSFormer are integrated into a unified framework and trained in an end-to-end manner.
Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed QSFormer for few-shot classification.

claim_records.text: Few-shot image classification aims to recognize novel classes given few labeled images from base classes.
Recent metric-learning few-shot image classification methods typically use a measure at only the image feature level.

fact_fields.method: recent metric-learning few-shot image classification methods

claim_records.text: Measuring similarity only at the image feature level may not be effective enough to generalize from base to novel classes when using only a few images.
The proposed multi-level correlation network (MLCN) for few-shot image classification effectively captures local information by taking a multi-level descriptor of an image into consideration.
MLCN includes a self-correlation module and a cross-correlation module to learn the semantic correspondence relation of local information based on learned representations.
MLCN includes a pattern-correlation module to capture the pattern of fine-grained images and find relevant structural patterns between base classes and novel classes.
Extensive experiments and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed MLCN method on four widely-used FSIC benchmarks.

claim_records.text: RS-MetaNet raises the level of learning from the sample to the task by organizing training in a meta way, and learns to learn a metric space that can well classify remote sensing scenes from a series of tasks.

The proposed Balance Loss maximizes the generalization ability of the model to new samples by maximizing the distance between different categories, providing scenes in different categories with better linear segmentation planes while ensuring model fit.
RS-MetaNet achieves state-of-the-art results in cases where there are only 1-20 labeled samples on the UCMerced_LandUse, NWPU-RESISC45, and Aerial Image Data datasets.

claim_records.text: Most approaches in few-shot learning rely on costly annotated data related to the goal task domain during (pre-)training.
Recently, unsupervised meta-learning methods have exchanged the annotation requirement for a reduction in few-shot classification performance.
In settings with realistic domain shift, common transfer learning has been shown to outperform supervised meta-learning.

ProtoTransfer constructs a metric embedding that clusters unlabeled prototypical samples and their augmentations closely together, and this pre-trained embedding serves as a starting point for few-shot classification by summarizing class clusters and fine-tuning.
ProtoTransfer outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on few-shot tasks from the mini-ImageNet dataset.
In few-shot experiments with domain shift, ProtoTransfer has comparable performance to supervised methods, but requires orders of magnitude fewer labels.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks built on the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized using pre-trained model parameters obtained via self-supervised learning.
STN applies Euclidean distance as the similarity measure for global features, and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as the similarity measure for local features.
STN integrates the two feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization to each metric, then weighting the normalized results to produce the final similarity score.
During the training phase, STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.
Experiments show the STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: Meta-Baseline performs meta-learning over a whole-classification pre-trained model on its evaluation metric, and achieves competitive performance to state-of-the-art methods on standard few-shot learning benchmarks.
Meta-learning learns the model from collections of few-shot classification tasks, which is believed to have a key advantage of making the training objective consistent with the testing objective.
Some recent works report that training for whole-classification (classification on the whole label-set) can get comparable or even better embedding than many meta-learning algorithms.

The edge between whole-classification models and meta-learning models in few-shot learning remains underexplored, and the effectiveness of meta-learning compared to whole-classification is still unclear.

Classifier-Baseline trains the whole-classification model with a linear layer on the top and applies cosine nearest-centroid metric during test time for few-shot classification on novel classes, without replacing the last layer with cosine classifier during training.
The Meta-Baseline is meta-learning over a converged Classifier-Baseline on its evaluation metric (cosine nearest-centroid).

Cosine classifier and Baseline++ perform whole-classification training by replacing the top linear layer with a cosine classifier, and adapt the classifier to few-shot classification tasks of novel classes by nearest centroid or fine-tuning a new layer respectively.
The effectiveness of whole-classification is revisited in two concurrent works with improved design choices.

claim_records.text: Discriminatively trained linear predictors can offer better generalization than nearest-neighbor classifiers even in the few-shot regime.

MetaOptNet uses discriminatively trained linear predictors as base learners to learn representations for few-shot learning, offering better tradeoffs between feature size and performance across a range of few-shot recognition benchmarks.

MetaOptNet exploits implicit differentiation of the optimality conditions of the convex problem and the dual formulation of the optimization problem to efficiently solve its objective, allowing use of high-dimensional embeddings with improved generalization at a modest increase in computational overhead.
MetaOptNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC100 few-shot learning benchmarks.

CIFAR-FS dataset consists of all 100 classes from CIFAR-100, randomly split into 64, 16 and 20 classes for meta-training, meta-validation, and meta-testing respectively, with each class containing 600 images of size 32 × 32.

FC100 dataset is derived from CIFAR-100, containing 100 classes grouped into 20 superclasses, partitioned into 60 classes from 12 superclasses for meta-training, 20 classes from 4 superclasses for meta-validation, and 20 classes from 4 superclasses for meta-testing.
Meta-learning approaches for few-shot learning can be broadly categorized into gradient-based methods and nearest-neighbor methods.
Prototypical networks represent each class by the mean embedding of the examples, and the classification rule is based on the distance to the nearest class mean.
Matching networks learn a kernel density estimate of the class densities using the embeddings over training data, and can be interpreted as a form of attention over training examples.

claim_records.text: The Multi-Space Prototypical Learning (MSPL) framework integrates Euclidean, Cosine, Chebyshev, and Wasserstein distances through a constrained weighting scheme to enhance embedding robustness and improve pattern recognition for few-shot network attack detection.
MSPL leverages Polyak-averaged prototype generation to stabilize the learning process and effectively adapt to rare and zero-day attacks.
MSPL uses an episodic training paradigm to ensure balanced representation across diverse attack classes, enabling robust generalization.
Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MSPL outperforms traditional approaches in detecting low-profile and novel attack types.

claim_records.text: Matching Networks improve one-shot accuracy on ImageNet from 87.6% to 93.2% compared to competing approaches.
Matching Networks improve one-shot accuracy on Omniglot from 88.0% to 93.8% compared to competing approaches.
The Matching Networks framework learns a network that maps a small labelled support set and an unlabelled example to its label, obviating the need for fine-tuning to adapt to new class types.
Matching Networks are capable of state-of-the-art performance on a variety of one-shot classification tasks.
As the support set S grows in size, the computation for each gradient update of the Matching Networks model becomes more expensive.
Random performance on an N-way k-shot learning task stands at 1/N.
One-shot experiments were run on three datasets: Omniglot, ImageNet, and Penn Treebank.
When trained solely on classes not in Lrand, Matching Nets improve upon Inception by almost 6% when tested on Lrand, halving the errors.
The Inception Oracle trained on all classes performs almost perfectly when restricted to 5 classes only.
The classifier defined by the Matching Networks equation is discriminative, requiring a sample to be sufficiently aligned with support set pairs sharing its label and misaligned with the rest.
The Matching Networks loss is simple and differentiable, allowing optimal parameters to be found in an end-to-end fashion.
A one-shot task on the Penn Treebank language modeling dataset demonstrates the usefulness of the same Matching Networks model on language modeling.

claim_records.text: Mutual Centralized Learning (MCL) associates each local feature with a particle that can bidirectionally random walk in a discrete feature space via affiliations.
MCL uses features' accessibility, defined as the expected number of visits to support features of a given class in a Markov process, to estimate class probability.
MCL achieves state-of-the-art performance on both miniImageNet and tieredImageNet few-shot classification benchmarks.
MCL can be plugged into existing few-shot learning methods by highlighting centralized local features.

claim_records.text: The proposed label-set synthesis method combines pairs of given examples in feature space to produce synthesized feature vectors corresponding to examples whose label sets are derived via set operations on the input pairs' label sets.
The proposed set operation based label manipulation generalizes to labels unseen during training, enabling augmentation on examples of novel categories for multi-label few-shot classifier learning.
The proposed method compares favorably to all common baselines on the newly proposed multi-label few-shot learning benchmark, as measured by classification and retrieval metrics.

claim_records.text: Most existing webly supervised learning methods focus on learning noise-robust models from web images while neglecting the performance drop caused by the differences between web domain and real-world domain.
The proposed Few-shot guided Prototypical (FoPro) representation learning method only needs a few labeled examples from reality and can significantly improve the performance in the real-world domain.
FoPro initializes each class center with few-shot real-world data as the realistic prototype.
FoPro narrows the intra-class distance between web instances and realistic prototypes by contrastive learning.
FoPro measures image-prototype distance with a learnable metric.
FoPro prototypes are polished by adjacent high-quality web images and involved in removing distant out-of-distribution samples.
FoPro is trained on web datasets with a few real-world examples guided and evaluated on real-world datasets.
FoPro achieves the state-of-the-art performance on three fine-grained datasets and two large-scale datasets.
Compared with existing WSL methods under the same few-shot settings, FoPro still excels in real-world generalization.

claim_records.text: Medical image interpretations are often obstructed by the paucity of data, unlike typical visual scene recognition domains where massive datasets are accessible to deep neural networks.
Different types of non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) are introduced in few-shot learning to address the data scarcity issue in medical image classification.
Extensive empirical studies validate the effectiveness of NMF, especially its supervised variants including discriminative NMF, and supervised and constrained NMF with sparseness.
NMF is compared with principal component analysis (PCA), the collaborative representation-based dimensionality reduction technique derived from eigenvectors.
With 14 different datasets covering 11 distinct illness categories, experimental results demonstrate that NMF is a competitive alternative to PCA for few-shot learning in medical imaging.
Supervised NMF algorithms are more discriminative in the subspace with greater effectiveness.
The part-based representation of NMF, especially its supervised variants, is dramatically impactful in detecting lesion areas in medical imaging with limited samples.

claim_records.text: The proposed patch-driven relational refinement learns cache adapter weights from intra-image patch dependencies rather than treating an image embedding as a monolithic vector.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

fact_fields.method: residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model proposed to achieve cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two steps: Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The designed RMP enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, ensuring better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

With the aid of CSRMs, the developed REP can strengthen the extracted features for those discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.

Extensive experiments conducted on five public fine-grained benchmarks demonstrate that HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios.
The code for HelixFormer is available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: In few-shot learning, the conventional pooled global feature is likely to lose useful local characteristics when classifying images under low-data regimes.

Existing deep descriptor-based FSL methods generally take all deep descriptors from neural networks into consideration, ignoring that some descriptors are useless in classification due to their limited receptive field.
Task-irrelevant descriptors could be misleading and multiple aggregative descriptors from background clutter could even overwhelm the object's presence in FSL.

A Mutual Nearest Neighbor (MNN) relation should be established to explicitly select the query descriptors that are most relevant to each task and discard less relevant ones from aggregative clutters in FSL.
Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DMN4) is proposed for few-shot learning.

fact_fields.method: Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network (DMN4)

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DMN4 outperforms the existing state-of-the-arts on both fine-grained and generalized datasets.
