assertions.source_quote: A second problem is choosing the right class representation without knowing the geometry of a novel class. Exemplar comparisons preserve individual support images but offer little aggregation; prototypes provide a compact mean-like summary but can collapse multimodal classes; distributions express uncertainty but require reliable distribution estimates; subspaces preserve variation or spatial structure but introduce singular-value decomposition, dimensionality, and template construction choices. These alternatives are complementary modeling biases, not a guaranteed progression toward a universally better classifier. The available evidence supports robustness or competitive accuracy for particular subspace and distributional designs, but not the conclusion that every few-shot class should be represented as a distribution or subspace. assertions.source_quote: The comparison function creates a related flexibility–generalization trade-off. Fixed Euclidean, cosine, nearest-prototype, or nearest-subspace rules are simple and stable, but they presuppose that one task-invariant geometric relation remains valid across episodes and classes. Learned nonlinear relation modules can express more complex compatibility between query and support features, but their extra capacity is trained on episodic tasks and must transfer to unseen classes; a scalar learned relation score is also less directly geometric than an explicit distance. Metric-agnostic conditional networks show that query-conditioned neural classifiers can perform well, but their authors distinguish that softmax-score architecture from a true metric, so it should be treated as a relational alternative rather than evidence that geometric comparison is obsolete. assertions.source_quote: Domain shift remains a concrete failure mode even when a metric succeeds on novel classes from the same benchmark. Metric-based encoders and metric functions can overfit feature distributions seen during episodic training and then fail on unseen domains; this is distinct from ordinary novel-class split generalization because image-feature distributions themselves change. Feature-wise transformation layers address the problem by simulating varied feature distributions and are described as method-agnostic add-ons for metric-based approaches, but the source also reports that their hyperparameters may require meticulous hand-tuning because cross-domain feature variation is difficult to model. Thus domain modulation adds both a potential robustness benefit and a tuning burden. assertions.source_quote: Evaluation fragmentation limits scientific comparison across the metric-learning literature. Papers report miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, CUB, Caltech-101, Dogs, Cars, FC100, Meta-Dataset, VTAB, SAR, and hyperspectral tasks, with different 1-shot or 5-shot, N-way, backbone, pretraining, episode-sampling, and adaptation settings. A gain on one protocol—such as the reported roughly two-percentage-point miniImageNet improvement from Proto-Triplet or ICNN losses, K-tuplet cross-dataset results, or best accuracy for metric methods in the FewSAR setting—cannot be converted into a general ranking when the methods were not run under matched data, architecture, and training budgets. This is a limitation of comparability, not proof that a missing method is ineffective. assertions.source_quote: Cross-family evaluation adds another unresolved issue: episodic metric learners and large-scale transfer learners optimize under different assumptions. The VTAB+Meta-Dataset study reports that carefully engineered large-scale BiT pretraining and fine-tuning is a remarkably competitive and robust few-shot baseline, and that BiT on average outperforms competing approaches on Meta-Dataset, while meta-learning approaches struggle on VTAB when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset. The same study also finds that pushing scale does not improve highly out-of-distribution Meta-Dataset tasks. Consequently, neither small episodic benchmark results nor large transfer results alone establish which metric mechanism is best; matched data scale, model capacity, fine-tuning, and test distribution are necessary for a fair comparison. assertions.source_quote: Richer embeddings improve available cues but impose their own costs and dependencies. K-tuplet and margin-style losses require informative sampling or careful intra-class and inter-class objectives; multi-stage networks add multiple outputs, self-attention, and learnable stage weights; global-local ViT branches add parameters and depend on pretrained, self-supervised features. These designs can counter the loss of shallow, local, or abstract information when a single pooled vector and single distance are used, but the source evidence does not imply that added branches always improve accuracy. Their trade-offs include training complexity, pretraining dependence, fusion-weight selection, and the risk of fitting benchmark-specific feature combinations. assertions.source_quote: Task heterogeneity challenges the common assumption of one shared metric across all episodes. A fixed metric can accommodate different class counts more naturally than some parameter-prediction meta-learners, but the Meta-Metric-Learner paper argues that a task-invariant metric is most plausible when tasks come from similar domains; realistic episodes may vary in class number, source domain, and task distribution. Its hybrid solution uses a meta-learner to specify a task-specific metric-based learner, improving flexibility at the cost of additional meta-learning machinery. This leaves an open choice between simple transferable metrics and adaptive metrics: the former are easier to deploy and inspect, while the latter require evidence that adaptation generalizes rather than overfits the training task distribution.
